Paths control supported distributions

Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort, September 2026. Checked once by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI), Ultra reasoning effort. Public domain (CC0).

Source/proof self-check and prerequisite integration by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Historical authorship and component terms are retained.

A distribution of order is usually bounded using derivatives on a neighborhood of its support. Can we use only their values on the support itself? For a general closed set, nearby points can carry incompatible Taylor data, so the divided remainders in Whitney's norm are essential. Paths inside the set can control those remainders. The length of the paths determines how many derivatives are needed.

We use Compatible jets on closed sets, especially its full Whitney norm and supported-distribution estimate, and Jets, supported distributions and local operators for smooth mollifiers, compact cutoffs and the canonical pairing with functions. The complete integral Taylor proof supplies the ambient Taylor estimates. The scalar foundation, §§12–13, proves Euclidean compactness, completeness, the intermediate value theorem, integration, differentiation and real powers. We prove the rectifiable-curve calculus and the required compactness of paths here. Exact source comparisons are recorded in the references.

Compactness of paths and elementary topology

Lemma 1.2 (a finite-grid compactness proof). Let have images in one bounded set and a common Lipschitz bound . Some subsequence converges uniformly to a continuous curve. If their Lipschitz bounds can be chosen as , the limit has Lipschitz bound and length at most .

Proof. Enumerate the dyadic points of , including its endpoints. At the first point, boundedness and Euclidean compactness give a subsequence with convergent values. Refine it for the second point and continue. The diagonal subsequence converges at every dyadic point. To see uniform convergence, fix a dyadic mesh . For each , choose a mesh point with . Two curves from this subsequence satisfy First make small, then use convergence at the finitely many mesh points. The subsequence is uniformly Cauchy. Completeness of supplies its pointwise limit, and the same uniform Cauchy bound gives uniform convergence to that limit. Passing to the limit in the Lipschitz inequality proves continuity. If , passing to the limit gives . Sum this inequality over any partition to obtain .

We also record the elementary connectedness facts used below. A continuous image of a connected set is connected: a separation of the image pulls back to a separation of the original set. Real intervals are connected by the intermediate value property, so convex sets are connected through their segments. The closure of a connected subset is connected: if that closure had a separation, density forces to meet both relatively open pieces, separating . A connected component is a maximal connected subset, so its closure is itself; components of a compact set are therefore compact. Distinct compact components have positive distance, because the continuous distance function attains its minimum on their product and a zero minimum would give a common point. With finitely many components, the minimum of these finitely many positive distances is positive.

Finally, a continuous injective map from a compact set into Euclidean space has continuous inverse on its image. Indeed, the image of each closed subset of the compact domain is compact, hence closed in Euclidean space. This is precisely the closed-set criterion for continuity of the inverse.

The derivative cost of a detour

Theorem 4.1 (pointwise jets on the support). Let be nonempty and compact, with finitely many connected components. Suppose that within each component every pair is joined by a rectifiable path in that component satisfying (1.2), with a common and .

In particular, for finitely many quasiconvex components, suffices.

Proof. The supported-distribution estimate in Compatible jets on closed sets, Corollary 4.1 bounds by a constant times the full norm of the restricted jet of . This jet is compatible because . We must bound all its order- normalized remainders by .

After division by , the first term is bounded because its exponent is

Every nonzero monomial in the second term has degree , where . Its coefficient is bounded by a constant times ; after division its remaining power is , bounded by one for . There are finitely many such terms. If , this polynomial difference is zero. Hence every normalized remainder is bounded by for these pairs.

For , use directly. Its derivative has terms of degrees through . Dividing each by leaves a nonpositive power of , and the endpoint term has that same denominator. Thus these remainders also have a bound .

Each connected component of a compact set is closed, hence compact. There are finitely many here, so distinct components have a positive minimum separation . For pairs in different components, the same direct polynomial estimate applies with . Its constant can depend on and the diameter. If there is only one component, this step is unnecessary.

Combining the estimates and the pointwise jet values proves

The preceding supported-distribution bound now gives (4.2). Multiplication by a smooth cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of does not change any of these jets or the pairing. This also proves the neighborhood version. Taking and gives the quasiconvex case.

The integer is a sufficient number of derivatives. The theorem does not claim that each distribution needs that many, or that this is the best bound for every set. In particular a point mass needs only the zeroth derivative, whatever larger-order class it is placed in.

The finite-component hypothesis also has a specific purpose: it controls pairs lying in different components. Infinitely many components can approach each other at arbitrarily small separations. Paths within the individual components say nothing about the Taylor remainders across those gaps.

Complete solutions

Solution 1. The segment lies in by convexity. For every partition its increment sum is , so its length is exactly that distance. Thus . A convex set is connected, so it has one connected component, and Theorem 4.1 applies with , . Nothing in the path Taylor proof requires interior points of . The derivatives are those of the ambient test function restricted to , so the same argument works for a segment, an affine disk, or a single point.

Solution 2. There is just one unordered pair, at distance , and

This proves (2.1) with , even without the derivative term. A continuous path in has connected image, and a connected subset of this two-point set is a singleton; alternatively the intermediate value theorem would force it to take value zero. The missing hypothesis is connectedness. Theorem 4.1 allows finitely many components. Each singleton satisfies its within-component path condition with a constant path, and their separation is . Hence it gives with . The two theorems address different questions: a path between every pair, and a distribution estimate that can also control finitely many separated pieces.

Solution 5. The curves have a common Lipschitz bound, for example , so they are equicontinuous. Since is compact, all their images lie in a fixed bounded neighborhood and hence in a common compact subset of Euclidean space. The finite-grid proof of Lemma 1.2 gives a uniformly convergent subsequence with continuous limit . Endpoints pass to the limit. For each ,

so closedness gives . For a partition, each increment of is at most times its parameter increment. The sum is therefore at most . Pass to the limit to get a sum at most ; taking the supremum over all partitions proves . Endpoints alone do not bound the length or give equicontinuity: a path between fixed endpoints can repeatedly traverse a loop, or make a large excursion, with arbitrarily large length. The uniform parametrized length control is what supports the compactness argument.
